question: What allows fungal elements to become visible in a KOH-prepared skin scraping?

answers.text: KOH digests keratin and human cellular debris while the chitinous fungal cell wall resists alkaline digestion, leaving fungal elements intact

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. KOH is a strong alkali that selectively dissolves keratin, dead corneocytes, and intercellular material, clearing the background. The fungal cell wall — composed largely of chitin — resists this alkaline digestion, so hyphae and yeast cells remain intact and stand out against the now-transparent field.

answers.text: KOH stains fungal hyphae a deep blue, making them visible against unstained human cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. KOH does not stain anything — it is a clearing agent, not a dye. Staining of fungal elements requires added dyes such as chlorazol black E or calcofluor white. The diagnostic principle is selective clearing, not staining.

answers.text: KOH selectively kills bacteria, leaving only fungi visible in the microscopy field

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. KOH does not act as a selective antimicrobial agent. It works by dissolving keratin and human cellular material — not by killing bacteria. The cleared field reveals fungal elements because their chitinous walls resist the alkali.

answers.text: KOH dissolves fungal cell walls, releasing a pigment that makes the organism visible

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. KOH does not dissolve the fungal cell wall — quite the opposite. The chitinous fungal wall resists KOH digestion, which is precisely why fungal elements survive intact. It is the human keratin that KOH dissolves.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the principle: KOH clears the field by digesting human keratin, while the chitinous fungal cell wall resists alkaline digestion and remains visible.
The selective clearing principle is the foundation of the KOH mount — chitin resists alkali while keratin does not.
